Of course! While the `caption` package is the standard and recommended way to customize captions, you can absolutely align them to the left without it by using some fundamental LaTeX commands.

The core idea is to place the caption text inside a box (like a `\parbox` or `minipage`) and control the alignment within that box.

Here are a few methods, starting with the most recommended non-package approach.

### Method 1: The Recommended Approach (Using a `minipage`)

This is the most robust and flexible method without using an extra package. You wrap your caption content in a `minipage` environment. This creates a self-contained "page within a page" where you can control formatting, like text alignment.

**How it works:**
1.  Inside `\caption{...}`, start a `minipage`.
2.  Give the `minipage` a width. `\linewidth` is a good choice as it will match the width of the surrounding text column.
3.  Use the `\raggedright` command inside the `minipage` to align the text to the left.

Here is a complete example:

```latex
\documentclass{article}
\usepackage{lipsum} % For dummy text

\begin{document}

\lipsum[1] % Some text to show alignment

\begin{table}[h!]
  \centering % This centers the table on the page
  \begin{tabular}{|l|c|r|}
    \hline
    Header 1 & Header 2 & Header 3 \\
    \hline
    Data A   & 123      & 45.67    \\
    Data B   & 456      & 89.01    \\
    \hline
  \end{tabular}
  
  % --- The Important Part ---
  \caption{%
    \begin{minipage}{\linewidth}
      \raggedright
      This is a very long caption designed to demonstrate left alignment without using the caption package. It will wrap to the next line and all lines will be aligned to the left margin of the caption block.
    \end{minipage}%
  }
  \label{tab:my_table}
\end{table}

\lipsum[2] % More text

\end{document}
```

**Result:**
The table itself will be centered on the page because of `\centering`, but the caption text will be typeset in a block the full width of the text area, with all lines aligned to the left.



### Method 2: A Simpler, Shorter Way (Using `\raggedright`)

For simple cases, you can often get away with just putting the `\raggedright` command directly inside the caption.

**How it works:**
The argument of `\caption{...}` forms a group. The `\raggedright` command is a switch that affects all subsequent text within its group.

```latex
\documentclass{article}

\begin{document}

\begin{table}[h!]
  \centering
  \begin{tabular}{|l|c|r|}
    \hline
    Column A & Column B \\
    \hline
    Item 1   & Item 2   \\
    \hline
  \end{tabular}
  
  \caption{\raggedright This is a left-aligned caption using the simpler \texttt{\textbackslash raggedright} method.}
  \label{tab:my_table_simple}
\end{table}

\end{document}
```

**Why Method 1 is often better:** The `minipage` approach gives you more explicit control over the width and behavior of the caption block, which can prevent unexpected formatting issues, especially with very long captions or in more complex layouts (like two-column documents). The simpler `\raggedright` method can sometimes have its width determined in ways that are surprising.

### Advanced Method: Redefining the Caption Command (Global Change)

This is a more advanced technique and is **not generally recommended** as it's a global change that will affect **all** figure and table captions in your document. But, it directly answers how to change the fundamental behavior.

You can redefine the internal LaTeX macro `\@makecaption`. This requires using `\makeatletter` and `\makeatother` because the command name contains an `@`.

```latex
\documentclass{article}
\usepackage{lipsum}

% --- Redefine the internal caption macro ---
\makeatletter
\long\def\@makecaption#1#2{%
  \vskip\abovecaptionskip
  % The original definition might try to center the text.
  % This new definition simply typesets it as a standard \noindent paragraph.
  \noindent\textbf{#1:} #2\par
  \vskip\belowcaptionskip}
\makeatother
% -----------------------------------------

\begin{document}

This change affects all captions globally.

\begin{table}[h!]
  \centering
  \begin{tabular}{|c|c|}
    \hline
    Test & Data \\
    \hline
  \end{tabular}
  % Now you don't need any special commands inside the caption
  \caption{This caption is now left-aligned by default due to the global redefinition. This applies to all tables and figures.}
  \label{tab:global_change}
\end{table}

\begin{figure}[h!]
    \centering
    \rule{5cm}{3cm} % A black box representing a figure
    \caption{This figure caption is also affected and is now left-aligned.}
    \label{fig:my_fig}
\end{figure}

\end{document}
```

### Why is the `caption` package usually recommended?

You specifically asked for a solution without it, but it's useful to know why it's the standard tool for this job:
*   **Separation of Content and Style:** You can set the justification for all captions in your preamble (`\usepackage[justification=raggedright]{caption}`) instead of adding formatting commands to every single caption.
*   **Simplicity:** The syntax is much cleaner and more readable.
*   **Rich Customization:** It provides easy options for changing the font, style of the label ("Table 1"), spacing, and much more, without needing to redefine complex internal macros.
